# Porting an xscreensaver hack

The rules live in `AGENTS.md` ("Rules", "Gotchas") and the path-scoped notes in
`.claude/rules/`. This skill sets the order of work and the points to stop. The
numbered steps are in `adding-a-hack.md` and the recipes it names are in
`techniques.md`, both next to this file. For several hacks in one go, read
`batches.md` too.

## 1. Pick, then read the source

Take S-rated rows from `docs/porting-assessment.md` first, and prefer a low
**Speed** band: the table runs each unported S hack on the host. The effort
rating counts missing shim calls, not memory, speed or stack (Braid was S, and
would have shown as high). A high band is a hack that will probably run slowly
on the board; a low band is not a guarantee, because a hack still doing
software `double` maths runs far slower on the device than on the host. Read
the hack's source before copying it, and look for:

| The source has | Technique (seen in) |
| --- | --- |
| Arrays or a state over a few MB | Build-time patch (Maze) |
| `sin`, `cos`, `sqrt`, `pow`, `double` in a hot loop | Single precision (Galaxy, Substrate) |
| Locals over a few KB | Stack check (Rorschach) |
| An allocation of 100 KB or more, or `exit()` on failure | Large allocations (Substrate) |
| Pixmaps, clip masks, a logo image | Images (Maze) |
| A hack that restarts itself | Restart leak test (Maze, Substrate) |
| A `free` that relies on state `draw` sets up (a lazy `initted`) | Stopping before the first draw (Blaster) |
| Hairlines, fades or `glPolygonOffset` in a GL hack | Thin lines in a GL hack |
| Threads, GL, Xft, shared memory | Skipping a hack |
| A licence header | Read it; add a notices section only if it differs from jwz's |

## 2. Set up

Work in a worktree off `origin/main`. Its setup and the commands it refuses are
in "Worktree setup".

## 3. Red, copy, green

Follow `adding-a-hack.md`. Show the registry test failing before
copying. Fill each shim gap test-first, then break the code on purpose and
watch the test fail ("Tests that cannot be fooled"). Filling a missing
function is a shim gap. Changing what every hack sees (the runner, a default, a
shared helper) is not: stop and ask Rod first.

## 4. Verify on the host

Run `pio test -e native`, `uv run --with pytest --with pillow pytest tools/tests`
and `uv run tools/check_notices.py`, and dump frames at several counts. Host
frames cannot show a byte swap, which happens in the push to the display: judge
colour on the device, on a colour you know the answer to.

## 5. Device

Flash only after Rod says so in this conversation; approval for one flash is
not approval for the next. See "Device capture". Report "compiles", "host tests
pass" and "runs on the device" separately; only Rod can say what the screen
shows. If it is slow, measure, change one thing, flash again and compare; if it
is still slow, say so and suggest dropping it. Record the numbers in
`tools/assessment_measured.md`, marking anything unmeasured as such.

## 6. Deliver

Commit named paths. Open the draft PR with `entire trail create` and put what
is unverified in its body. After a rebase, a push needs `--force-with-lease`:
ask Rod each time. Rod approves and merges; then delete the branch and
fast-forward `main`. New gotchas go in the matching `.claude/rules/` file (or
`AGENTS.md` if they apply everywhere) in the same PR, and deferred
ideas become issues.

## Red flags

| Thought | Reality |
| --- | --- |
| "It is rated S, so I need not read it" | Maze was rated L for Xlib gaps; the real blocker was a 20 MB `calloc`. |
| "It compiles, so it works" | Rorschach compiled and rebooted on its first frame. |
| "The colours look right" | Not from a host frame: every hack was byte swapped until Maze. |
| "My test passes, so it tests something" | A test through Pyro passed with the runner broken. Break the code on purpose. |
| "AGENTS.md says to fix shim gaps, so I can change the runner" | A new function is a gap. A change every hack sees needs Rod. |
| "Rod approved flashing earlier" | Ask again for each flash. |

# Porting a batch of hacks

For several hacks on one branch, with Rod away. The per-hack steps are in
`SKILL.md` and `adding-a-hack.md`; this is what a batch adds. Per-hack findings
live in `.claude/rules/hacks.md`, not here.

## Order of work

1. Read every header before copying anything: a `(GPL)` tag or an xlock notice
   changes the notices row, and a licence that is not a permission notice means
   stop and ask.
2. Triage by gap count. Do the easy ones first: they pay for shim gaps the
   others need. Leave GL and anything under a few fps to last.
3. One branch, a commit per hack, shim code test-first and mutation-checked.
   No PR until Rod says.
4. `uv run tools/wire_hack.py <name> <Class> "<copyright>"` copies the file and
   registers it with a frame hash of `0` (skipped), so every commit stays green.
   Then `pio run -e dump`, fill the gaps, dump frames at several counts and
   look at them.
5. Flash and measure each hack as soon as it runs
   (`bash tools/flash_and_capture.sh <hack> 30`). Report measured, unjudged and
   unseen separately.
6. Pin all the new hashes in one run, after looking at the frames:
   `HACK_PINS_OUT=<file> pio test -e native -f test_hacks`.
7. Measured rows, rules, a regenerated assessment, and a notes file for Rod: what
   to look at, which choices are his, what was not measured.

## Traps

| Trap | Do |
| --- | --- |
| A change that is not pixel-identical by construction (single precision, a faster fill) and you only checked fps | Look at a frame. A hack drew garbage for hours at "20 fps" |
| `#define double float` before a header that has `double` in a struct a shim `.c` shares | Include that header first, then the define; a flat-screen test guards it |
| A hack that keeps state in statics across starts | Its pin depends on earlier tests; reset the static in a wrapper, and test both outcomes |
| A mode picked with `random()` | A boot is deterministic, so measure the other mode by forcing it |
| Constants in pixels or frames, tuned for another window size or frame rate | Scale them at build time (`tools/fireworkx_patch.py`), not by editing the copy |
| A hack that treats `malloc(0) == NULL` as out of memory | The board returns NULL for zero bytes, the host a pointer: it stops drawing on the board only. Reproduce with an allocator hook that fails for zero |
| A stop that leaks | `MallocStackLogging=1 leaks --atExit -- .pio/build/dump/program <index> 0 out.raw` names the line (rebuild `-e dump` first) |

## Finding the cost

Skip one thing behind a temporary flag and read `step=`; revert it. Guessing
was wrong three times running. The usual causes here:

- full-frame passes over PSRAM: a clear, a copy, a blur, a 565 conversion (render
  smaller, alias a pixmap to the window, erase only what was drawn)
- the shim's polygon fill, which divides in double (`hacks/float_polygon.h`)
- soft double: `xtensa-esp32s3-elf-nm <object> | grep ' U __.*df'`; `frand` hides
  a `1.0` in its macro body (`hacks/single_frand.h`)
- a pause the hack asks for (`wait=`): override `*delay` and say the pace changed

## Choices for Rod

When look and speed trade off, leave a build flag per option, measure each, and
register the one nearer his bar. After his hands-on notes, expect to retune.

## Tools

| Need | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Register a hack | `tools/wire_hack.py` |
| Flash a pinned build and read the serial log | `tools/flash_and_capture.sh`, `tools/serial_capture.py` |
| Does a test notice a break | `tools/mutate.py <file> 'old=>new' --cmd '...'` |
| Pin hashes | `HACK_PINS_OUT` (above) |
# Adding a hack

Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md. The order of work is in `SKILL.md`.

The `port-hack` skill orders this work, says what to read for before copying a
hack, and holds a recipe per trap. The steps:

1. Check its row in `docs/porting-assessment.md` (effort and Speed band) and
   read its licence header.
2. Update the expected list in `firmware/test/test_hacks/test_hacks.c` and see
   it fail.
3. Copy the file to `firmware/src/hacks/<name>/<name>.c`, add the notices row
   and an `extern` plus entry in `hacks/registry.c`.
4. Fill shim gaps test-first in `firmware/test/test_xshim/`. The compile
   check in `score_hacks.py` shows what is missing.
5. Host tests pass, dump a frame and look at it, then (with Rod's go-ahead)
   flash and measure fps and free heap/PSRAM over serial. To pin its frame
   hash after looking at the frame, put `0x1ull` in `kBaseline`, run
   `pio test -e native -f test_hacks`, convert the "Was N" in the failure line
   with `python3 -c "print(hex(N))"`, and run it again.
6. Regenerate the assessment and add measurements to
   `tools/assessment_measured.md`, then re-run the speed backtest: each port
   adds a point to the check of the Speed bands, which were fitted to the first
   29 hacks. To make a port a real test, commit its host time and predicted
   range first (`docs/speed-predictions.md` shows the form), flash it as copied,
   and add its name to `HOLDOUT` in `tools/speed_backtest.py`. The first four
   (Mountain, Epicycle, Kaleidescope, Celtic) all fell where predicted.
7. If a hack is slow and `double`-heavy (many `double`s, `sqrt`, `sin`/`cos`,
   `pow`), try a single-precision wrapper like `hacks/galaxy_single.c` (for a
   plain screenhack, `hacks/substrate_single.c`; the recipe is in the skill's
   `techniques.md`), and compare double and float frames at several frame
   counts. A resource
   override can skip a hack's restart cleanup: Galaxy leaked at `count: 2`, so
   leak-test any override.
8. If Rod drops a port after seeing it (Celtic): remove it from `g_hacks[]`, the
   expected list, its hash and its leak test; keep the source and notices row;
   add `name: reason` (short: it is printed as a bullet) to
   `tools/failed_ports.txt`; file an issue.

# Per-hack gotchas

Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.

- Maze keeps a 1000 by 1000 maze and three 1,000,000-entry move lists in one
  `calloc` (about 20 MB; the board has 8 MB of PSRAM). `hacks/maze/maze.c`
  stays byte-identical: `firmware/patch_maze.py` (a PlatformIO `pre:` script
  in every env) writes a copy with both limits at 80 into the build dir, using
  `tools/maze_patch.py`, which fails loudly if upstream's `#define`s change.
  `hacks/maze_small.c` includes that copy and the original is excluded from
  `build_src_filter`. A `gridSize` below 7 would overflow the 80 by 80 arrays.
- Pacman has two build-time patches (`tools/pacman_patch.py`, run by
  `firmware/patch_pacman.py`; wrappers `hacks/pacman_stdlevel.c` and
  `hacks/pacman_loop_ai.c`): it always plays the fixed level, because the
  random generator recursed to ~315 KB and boot-looped the board, and the
  ghosts' route search is a loop (it was 453 levels deep). Each patch checks
  what it replaces. Its sprite sheet is built from `vendor/` into the build dir
  by `firmware/pacman_sprites.py` and never committed (3 MB as C text).
- Braid runs at 3-9 fps (0.8-2 before four rounds of work): it redraws every
  segment of the braid each frame to spin the colours. A host profile put its
  disc fill at 6% and the board spent most of its time there, because the Mac
  does `double` at full speed. Split a slow hack's step on the device with a
  temporary flag that returns early from the expensive call.
- Maze fills the whole 466 by 466 square, so its corners and the exit marker
  fall outside the round display's visible circle.
- `check_notices.py` reads 100 lines of header: Maze's licence follows a long
  modification history.
- A hack can be freed before its first draw: two quick presses, or a press
  with the 90 s rotation. `test_every_hack_can_be_stopped_before_its_first_frame`
  runs every hack through it. Blaster's free dereferenced NULL (it sizes a loop
  in init but allocates in draw), so `hacks/blaster_safe.c` includes the
  unmodified hack with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` emptied and registers it with a
  free that zeroes `NUM_ROBOTS` when `robots` is NULL.
- Deluxe is built through `hacks/deluxe_opaque.c`, which includes the unmodified
  hack with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` emptied and registers it with overrides:
  `*transparent: False` (upstream's plane masks need colour planes, which
  `allocate_alpha_colors` reports none of) and `*doubleBuffer: False` (it was
  added when the shim drew only on the canvas, so the `XCopyArea` from its
  blank pixmap erased the picture; pixmaps work now, but two 434 KB back
  buffers and a full-frame copy each frame would cost more than they give).
  The wrapper then gives each throbber's GC an alpha of 26
  of 32 (upstream's translucent weight) and sends full wide circles to
  `stroke_circle`. A plain screenhack's `HackEntry` has no overrides unless a
  wrapper builds it. Its step is 45-63 ms on the device against a 32.5 ms push,
  so about 11-13 fps; ideas for more are in issue #54.
- Eight of the S-hack batch (Anemone, Anemotaxis, Compass, FuzzyFlakes,
  Halftone, Interaggregate, LMorph, Wormhole) are built through
  `hacks/<name>_direct.c` (pixmap double buffering, see `techniques.md`;
  LMorph's is `lmorph_single.c` because it needs no `HAVE_JWXYZ`). All but
  Anemotaxis and Wormhole, and Euler2D (`euler2d_single.c`), also use
  `single_precision.h` plus build-time float literals (`patch_float_literals.py`
  lists them). `single_precision.h` leaves `floor` and `ceil` on the double
  versions: Euler2D's wrapper maps them itself. After the literal pass, `nm`
  still shows soft-double helpers in Euler2D, Halftone, Interaggregate and
  Anemone; their source was not chased.
- `test_frames_of_every_hack_but_maze_match_main` stops at the first hash that
  differs, in registry order, so repinning several hacks takes one test run
  each (about 85 s), earliest first. A hack whose frames do not change under a
  wrapper (Compass and Halftone in single precision) keeps its hash.
- Anemone's step moves between 31 and 56 ms as its arms grow and shrink, so its
  fps is 11 to 15.5 whatever one 20 s window says. Forest waits 500 ms between
  trees by design (about 2 fps, and the push is 88 rows).
- A hack that unpacks pixel values itself (Substrate and Interaggregate, in
  their `point2rgb`) assumes ordinary RGB565, but the canvas holds the bytes
  swapped. Its wrapper swaps pixels where they cross `XAllocColor` and
  `XSetForeground`. Interaggregate shipped without this: its alpha blends
  mixed the wrong bit fields and drew rainbow noise instead of green and brown
  strokes. `test_interaggregate_blend` includes the wrapper to check one blend.
- `dump` never seeds `random()`, so a hack that picks a mode at start (Truchet,
  12 modes) shows the same one in every dump. To see others, build the hack
  alone (`probe_hacks.registry_source` and `shim_sources`) from a copy outside
  `vendor/`, with a `__attribute__((constructor))` that calls
  `srandom(atoi(getenv("SEED")))`. A device boot is deterministic too (Halo
  chose Ramp on five boots in a row), so a hack that picks a mode with
  `random()` always starts the same one: force another with a temporary
  `*mode:` override to measure it. Rotation reaches other modes because the
  random state differs by then.
- Hexadrop (`hexadrop_single.c`) runs at about 10 fps, under the 15 fps bar.
  Splitting its step on the device showed the maths and the edge walk cost
  0.1 ms and all the rest is canvas writes: about 860 KB of 16-bit stores
  into the PSRAM canvas a frame. Single precision, a float convex fill and
  two-pixel stores took it from 2.4 to 10.2 fps with pixel-identical frames.
  More needs a shared canvas change or rasterising in row bands.
- Halo (`halo_direct.c`, `halo_planes.h`, `halo_circles.h`) draws whole circles
  into 1-bit pixmaps and XORs two of them. Its pixmaps are packed bit planes
  (27 KB each), not colour pixmaps: 434 KB colour stand-ins made Seuss mode
  (three runs in four) 5-9 fps, because window-sized circles are millions of
  PSRAM writes, and a float circle fill alone changed nothing. A device boot
  is deterministic, so every boot picked Ramp mode and hid that: force
  `*colorMode: seuss` temporarily to measure the other mode. It overrides
  `*delay` to 10 ms (upstream asks for 100 ms), so the circles grow faster.
- StonerView's seven files are built as one unit by `stonerview_gl.c`.
  Upstream never frees its oscillator list ("how do we free this?"), so the
  wrapper frees it through the `next` links before upstream's release.
- XMatrix needs `matrix_glyphs.py` (a `pre:` script in every env), which
  converts four PNGs from `vendor/` into blobs in the build directory: they
  are never committed (1.5 MB of C text each for the large sheets). It
  registers through `xmatrix_direct.c` with `*trace: False`, which skips the
  typed "connecting" sequence it would open with (the rare "Knock, knock,
  Neo" event, `knockKnock`, is still on); `*matrixFont: small`
  gives 46 columns instead of 23. Its text modes read no text: the
  `textclient.h` stand-in never opens a source, and Xt timers never fire.
- Flurry is not ported. It draws 3,600 blended, textured quads a frame and
  needs `glAlphaFunc`, `glRectd`, `gluBuild2DMipmaps` and luminance-alpha
  textures, none in TinyGL here. With `gl_budget.py`'s per-vertex and
  per-pixel costs that is well under 1 fps (arithmetic, not a measurement:
  the tool cannot read a multi-file hack).
- Qix and Fireworkx both leaked on every stop, found by the restart leak test.
  Qix's `qix_free` skips each segment's `lines[i].p` array (about 48 KB per
  stop); Fireworkx below 24 bits never frees its own 565 image buffer (48 KB).
  Their wrappers (`qix_direct.c`, `fireworkx_single.c`) free the missing piece
  before calling upstream's free. LeakSanitizer does not run on macOS, but
  `MallocStackLogging=1 leaks --atExit -- .pio/build/dump/program <index> 0
  out.raw` names the allocating line in seconds (rebuild `-e dump` first: a
  `pio test` deletes the program).
- Starfish and Goop spent most of a frame in the shim's polygon fill (double
  maths per edge per row). `hacks/float_polygon.h` fills any even-odd polygon
  in float, optionally mixed in at an alpha in 32nds (all three colour
  channels with one multiply), and took Starfish from 8.5 to 19 fps. Goop draws
  straight onto the window (its `XCreatePixmap` is the window and the
  `XCopyArea` is skipped) and blends each blob in at the alpha upstream's jwxyz
  path uses. Its full-frame clear cost 15 ms, so `hacks/span_erase.h` erases
  only the bounding boxes the blobs filled last frame (pixel-identical frames):
  14.6-15.2 fps translucent. The shared `canvas_fill_polygon` is still double
  (Hexadrop has its own convex float fill). Goop is built through
  `goop_direct.c` with `HAVE_JWXYZ`; the colour-plane path needs planes the
  canvas lacks.
- A wrapper that does `#define double float` must include any header with a
  `double` in a struct the shim's `.c` files also use BEFORE the define: the
  hack includes it again, the guard keeps the copy seen through the macro, and
  the two sides disagree on the layout. `spline.h` did this to Starfish and
  Goop: they drew garbage (flat colours) at 16-20 fps and their first pinned
  hashes were of it. Look at a frame after any change that is not
  pixel-identical by construction;
  `test_hacks_that_use_the_spline_draw_a_real_picture` now fails on a flat
  screen.
- Fireworkx renders at 1/`FIREWORKX_SCALE` of the width and height
  (`hacks/lowrez_put.h`: it is told the window is smaller and `XPutImage`
  draws each pixel as a square): 2.4 fps as copied, 11 at a scale of 3, 12.4 at
  4. Its glow, flash pass and 565 conversion are full-frame walks over PSRAM.
  Its header says "(GPL)" but the text is the standard permission notice.

"""Check that every copied third-party source has a licence notice and is
listed in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md.

Run with: uv run tools/check_notices.py
"""

import argparse
import sys
from pathlib import Path

# Copied third-party code: one directory per hack under hacks/ (top-level
# files in hacks/ are our own, e.g. the registry), plus xs_support/.
SUFFIXES = {".c", ".h", ".cpp"}
HEADER_LINES = 100
NOTICE_PHRASES = (
    "permission to use, copy, modify, distribute, and sell this software",
    "permission is hereby granted, free of charge",
    "permission to use, copy, modify, and distribute this software",
)


def has_notice(text: str) -> bool:
    lines = (line.lstrip(" \t/*") for line in text.splitlines()[:HEADER_LINES])
    head = " ".join(" ".join(lines).split()).lower()
    return "copyright" in head and any(p in head for p in NOTICE_PHRASES)


def check(src_dir: Path, notices_md: Path) -> list[str]:
    notices = notices_md.read_text() if notices_md.exists() else ""
    problems = []
    candidates = sorted((src_dir / "hacks").glob("*/**/*")) + sorted(
        (src_dir / "xs_support").rglob("*")
    )
    for path in candidates:
        if path.suffix not in SUFFIXES or not path.is_file():
            continue
        rel = path.relative_to(src_dir)
        if not has_notice(path.read_text(errors="replace")):
            problems.append(f"{rel}: no licence notice in first {HEADER_LINES} lines")
        if path.name not in notices and path.stem not in notices:
            problems.append(f"{rel}: not listed in {notices_md.name}")
    # TinyGL's sources carry no per-file header, so it is checked as a
    # directory: its LICENSE beside the sources, and a mention in the notices.
    tinygl = src_dir / "tinygl"
    if tinygl.is_dir():
        if not (tinygl / "LICENSE").is_file():
            problems.append("tinygl: no LICENSE file")
        if "TinyGL" not in notices:
            problems.append(f"tinygl: not mentioned in {notices_md.name}")
    return problems


def main(argv: list[str]) -> int:
    root = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("--src", default=str(root / "firmware" / "src"))
    parser.add_argument("--notices", default=str(root / "THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md"))
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)
    problems = check(Path(args.src), Path(args.notices))
    for problem in problems:
        print(problem)
    return 1 if problems else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main(sys.argv[1:]))

# GitHub Flavored Markdown Generation

**Version:** 1.2.1

Generate GFM that passes markdownlint validation with zero violations.

## Core Principles

### 1. Blank Lines Are Mandatory

- Before/after ALL lists (MD032)
- Before/after ALL headings except document start (MD022)
- Before/after ALL code blocks (MD031)
- Between ALL block-level elements

### 2. Consistency Required

- Use `-` for lists
- Use `#` for headings (ATX)
- Regular spaces only—never tabs/nbsp

### 3. Structure Matters

- Heading hierarchy: 1→2→3 (not 1→3)
- ONE H1 per document
- Files end with one newline
- Lines under 80 chars

### 4. Invisible Characters Matter

- Use ONLY regular spaces (U+0020)
- Never non-breaking spaces (U+00A0,  )
- Never tabs
- UTF-8 encoding

## Pre-Generation Checklist

- [ ] Where will lists/headings/code appear?
- [ ] Heading levels verified (1→2→3)?
- [ ] Using `-` for all lists?
- [ ] Code languages specified?
- [ ] Lines under 80 chars?
- [ ] Line breaks needed? (two trailing spaces)
- [ ] Using regular spaces only?
- [ ] URLs wrapped in `<>` or `[]`?
- [ ] Document starts with H1?
- [ ] Ordered lists use `1.` for all items?
- [ ] File ends with single newline?
- [ ] Tables use consistent spacing?

## Essential Rules

### Lists (MD032, MD004)

```markdown
Text before.

- Item one
- Item two

Text after.
```

### Headings (MD001, MD022)

```markdown
Text.

## Heading

Content.
```

### Code Blocks (MD031, MD040)

````markdown
Text.

```python
code()
```

Text.
````

**Nested Fences:** When showing markdown examples that contain code blocks,
use **one more backtick** than the deepest level:

- Three backticks (` ``` `): Regular code
- Four backticks (` ```` `): Markdown examples with code
- Five backticks (` ````` `): Nested markdown examples

`````markdown
````markdown
# Example

```bash
command
```

````
`````

### Line Length (MD013)

Break long lines at natural points. Use reference-style links for long URLs.

### URLs and Email (MD034)

Wrap bare URLs and emails:

```markdown
Wrong: https://example.com
Right: <https://example.com>
Right: [link](https://example.com)

Wrong: user@example.com
Right: <user@example.com>
```

### Document Structure (MD041)

Start with H1 (or front matter then H1):

```markdown
# Document Title

First paragraph.
```

### Ordered Lists (MD029)

Use `1.` for all items:

```markdown
1. First
1. Second
1. Third
```

### File Endings (MD047)

End with single newline:

```text
Last content line.
[single newline]
[EOF]
```

### Table Column Style (MD060)

Use consistent spacing in tables. Three styles:

**Compact (recommended):** `| cell |` - single space around content

```markdown
| Header 1 | Header 2 |
| --- | --- |
| Data | More data |
```

**Aligned:** Pipes vertically aligned with padding

**Tight:** `|cell|` - no spaces

Pick ONE style per document. Compact is preferred.

### Character Encoding

**Detection:** View → Render Whitespace in VS Code

**Fix:** Find `\u00A0` → Replace with space

**Critical for AI:** Two trailing spaces = intentional line breaks. Do NOT
remove them.

## Critical Error Patterns

### 1. List Without Blank Lines

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD032 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
Text:
- Item
Text.
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD032 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
Text:

- Item

Text.
```

### 2. Heading Without Blank Lines

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD022 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
Text.
## Head
Text.
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD022 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
Text.

## Head

Text.
```

### 3. Code Without Blanks/Language

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD031 MD040 -->

**Wrong:**

````markdown
Text:
```
code
```
Text.
````

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD031 MD040 -->

**Right:**

````markdown
Text:

```python
code
```

Text.
````

### 4. Inconsistent Markers

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD004 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
- Item
* Item
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD004 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
- Item
- Item
```

### 5. Skipping Levels

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD001 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
# Title

### Sub (skipped H2)
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD001 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
# Title

## Section

### Sub
```

## Post-Generation Validation

1. Lists have blank lines before/after
2. Headings have blank lines before/after
3. Code has blank lines before/after
4. Heading progression: 1→2→3→4
5. All lists use `-`
6. All code has language
7. Lines under 80 chars
8. Document starts with H1
9. URLs wrapped properly
10. Ordered lists use `1.`
11. File ends with one newline
12. Two trailing spaces used intentionally
13. Only regular spaces (no nbsp/tabs)
14. Tables use consistent column spacing

## Mental Model

Markdown is **blocks with mandatory spacing:**

```text
[Text Block]
↓ BLANK LINE ↓
[Heading Block]
↓ BLANK LINE ↓
[List Block]
↓ BLANK LINE ↓
[Code Block]
↓ BLANK LINE ↓
[Text Block]
[EOF]
```

Every block transition = blank line required.

## Quick Patterns

**List:**

```markdown
text

- item

text
```

**Heading:**

```markdown
text

## Head

text
```

**Code:**

````markdown
text

```lang
code
```

text
````

**Nested:**

```markdown
- parent
  - child
- parent
```

**Ordered:**

```markdown
text

1. item
1. item

text
```

**Table:**

```markdown
text

| Header | Header |
| --- | --- |
| Cell | Cell |

text
```

## Common Languages

**Programming:** `python` `javascript` `java` `c` `cpp` `go` `rust` `ruby`
`php` `swift` `kotlin` `typescript`

**Shell:** `bash` `sh` `powershell` `cmd` `zsh`

**Markup:** `html` `css` `xml` `json` `yaml` `toml` `markdown`

**Database:** `sql` `postgresql` `mysql`

**Other:** `text` `diff` `log`

## Validation

```bash
markdownlint filename.md
```

Goal: Zero errors/warnings.

## Additional Resources

See bundled references:

- `references/complete-rules.md` - Full rule catalog
- `references/edge-cases.md` - Platform quirks
- `references/examples.md` - Detailed examples

## Remember

Most common: Missing blank lines around lists/headings/code.

**Two trailing spaces:** Intentional line breaks. Do NOT remove.

When in doubt:

1. Add blank lines before/after blocks
2. Use `-` for lists
3. Use `#` for headings
4. Specify code language
5. Increment headings by one
6. Use regular spaces only
7. Two trailing spaces = line break

#!/bin/bash
# Flashes a build that starts on one hack with rotation off, then reads the
# serial log. Needs the board, and Rod's say-so in the session (AGENTS.md:
# never flash without asking, unless he has said it is allowed).
#
#   bash tools/flash_and_capture.sh <hack> <seconds> [extra build flags] [lines]
#
# <hack> is a name from g_hacks[] in any case; extra flags are things like
# "-DFIREWORKX_SCALE=2"; the last `run` lines (default 6) are printed. The full
# log and the flash output go to $OUT_DIR (default: ./flash-capture, which
# should be somewhere git ignores, such as your scratchpad).
set -u
[ $# -ge 2 ] || { sed -n '2,12p' "$0"; exit 2; }
hack=$1 seconds=$2 extra=${3:-} lines=${4:-6}
repo=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)
out=${OUT_DIR:-./flash-capture}
mkdir -p "$out"
out=$(cd "$out" && pwd)

source "$repo/tools/env.sh"
cd "$repo/firmware" || exit 1
PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS="-DSTART_HACK=\\\"$hack\\\" -DROTATE_SECONDS=0 $extra" \
  NO_COLOR=1 pio run -e stopwatch -t upload > "$out/flash_$hack.txt" 2>&1
pio_status=$?
unset PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS
verified=$(grep -c 'Hash of data verified' "$out/flash_$hack.txt")
echo "flash verified: $verified" "$(grep -E 'Flash:' "$out/flash_$hack.txt")"
grep -E "error:|overflowed" "$out/flash_$hack.txt" | head -3
# A failed flash leaves the old firmware running, and the capture would measure
# that: stop rather than report numbers for the wrong build.
if [ "$pio_status" -ne 0 ] || [ "$verified" -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "flash failed (pio exit $pio_status, $verified verified); see $out/flash_$hack.txt" >&2
  exit 1
fi
echo "note: the board now starts on $hack with rotation off; flash a normal build when done"
"$repo/.venv/bin/python" -I "$repo/tools/serial_capture.py" "$out/$hack.log" "$seconds"
grep -a "^run" "$out/$hack.log" | tail -"$lines" | cut -c1-125

"""PlatformIO pre-build script: writes the copies of hacks with their decimal
literals made floats that src/hacks/*_single.c include. See
tools/float_literals.py for why."""

import sys
from pathlib import Path

Import("env")  # noqa: F821

project = Path(env["PROJECT_DIR"])  # noqa: F821
sys.path.insert(0, str(project.parent / "tools"))
import float_literals  # noqa: E402
import fireworkx_patch  # noqa: E402

generated = Path(env.subst("$BUILD_DIR")) / "generated"  # noqa: F821
generated.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

for name in ("braid",) + ('euler2d', 'compass', 'fuzzyflakes', 'halftone', 'interaggregate', 'anemone', 'lmorph', 'hexadrop', 'fireworkx', 'starfish', 'goop'):
    source = (project / "src" / "hacks" / name / f"{name}.c").read_text()
    if name == "fireworkx":
        source = fireworkx_patch.scale_for_a_small_window(source)
    patched = float_literals.float_literals(source)
    target = generated / f"{name}_floatlit.c"
    if not target.exists() or target.read_text() != patched:
        target.write_text(patched)

env.Append(CPPPATH=[str(generated)])  # noqa: F821

/* Builds the unmodified compass.c in single precision (the ESP32-S3's FPU is
 * single-precision only, so `double` maths runs in software) and
 * with its decimal literals made floats at build time
 * (tools/float_literals.py), or `0.5 * x` would stay software double, with HAVE_JWXYZ
 * defined after the framework headers. Upstream defines it where the window
 * system double-buffers for the hack, and the hack then draws straight on the
 * window. The shim can draw into pixmaps, but a back buffer would cost 434 KB
 * and a full-frame copy each frame, and would dirty every row. */
#include <math.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>

#include "screenhack.h"

#include "hacks/single_precision.h"

#undef XSCREENSAVER_MODULE
#define XSCREENSAVER_MODULE(CLASS, PREFIX)
#define HAVE_JWXYZ
#undef M_PI
#define M_PI 3.14159265358979323846f

#include "compass_floatlit.c"

const HackEntry compass_hack = {"Compass", compass_defaults, compass_init,
                                compass_draw, compass_free, NULL, NULL};
/* Included by the *_single.c wrappers just before the unmodified hack source,
 * after every header the hack needs, so shared structs keep their `double`
 * layout. The ESP32-S3's FPU is single-precision only: `double` and the double
 * libm calls run in software. */
#ifndef HACKS_SINGLE_PRECISION_H
#define HACKS_SINGLE_PRECISION_H

#define double float
#define sqrt(x) sqrtf(x)
#define sin(x) sinf(x)
#define cos(x) cosf(x)
#define atan(x) atanf(x)
#define atan2(y, x) atan2f(y, x)
#define exp(x) expf(x)
#define fabs(x) fabsf(x)
#define fmod(x, y) fmodf(x, y)
#define pow(x, y) powf(x, y)
#define log(x) logf(x)

_Static_assert(sizeof(double) == sizeof(float),
               "single_precision.h must be in effect");

#endif

"""Mutation-checks a file: breaks it one way at a time, runs the tests, and
reports whether they noticed.

    uv run tools/mutate.py <file> '<old>=><new>' ['<old>=><new>' ...] \\
        [--cmd 'pio test -e native -f test_float_polygon'] [--cwd firmware]

Each mutation replaces the first `<old>` in the file with `<new>`. A mutation is

- CAUGHT if the command fails with a test failure, a sanitizer report or a
  crash,
- BUILD ERROR if it fails without one (the mutation broke the compile: it proves
  nothing, so write a smaller one),
- SURVIVED if the command passes: the tests cannot tell the code from the
  broken code. Either a test is missing, or the mutation is equivalent (it
  changes nothing observable: say so rather than adding a test).

The file is always restored, and the run says so. Use `source tools/env.sh`
first for the default `pio` command. A multi-line mutation can be written with
real newlines inside the quotes.
"""

)

    "Program received signal",  # a test crashed (ASan aborts print this under pio)
)

git branch --show-current && git add THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md firmware/platformio.ini firmware/src/hacks/registry.c firmware/src/hacks/moire2 firmware/src/hacks/moire2_direct.c firmware/src/hacks/moire2_planes.h firmware/src/x11shim/xshim.c firmware/src/x11shim/xshim.h firmware/test/test_hacks/test_hacks.c firmware/test/test_xshim/test_xshim.c firmware/test/test_moire2_planes && git status --short && git commit -q -m "Port Moire2 on bit planes; record a GC's function

The shim now remembers a GC's function (GXcopy, GXor, GXxor) without changing
how it draws. Moire2 draws outline circles into four depth-1 pixmaps and merges
them with OR or XOR, so its wrapper keeps them as packed bit planes
(moire2_planes.h, on Halo's). The first version took 54 ms a frame: 64-bit
index maths in the plane copy and a per-pixel expansion. Both now work in
32 bits and a byte at a time (28 ms), and the 50 ms delay is overridden to
10 ms, so it runs at 16 fps.

# GL layer and TinyGL gotchas

OpenGL hacks run on TinyGL, a software OpenGL (C-Chads fork, commit
`36a7987`, zlib-style licence). Issues #42 to #46 hold the numbers and ideas.

- `src/tinygl/` is byte-identical to upstream and excluded from every env.
  `firmware/patch_tinygl.py` runs `tools/tinygl_patch.py` and writes the
  patched tree, plus one unity file, into `.pio/build/<env>/generated/`;
  `glshim/tinygl_build.c` compiles it. Each patch checks its anchor and fails
  with "has upstream changed?". TinyGL's README allows building it as one
  unit, and it compiles cleanly that way.
- A GL hack gets `USE_GL` from a one-line wrapper: `hacks/<name>_gl.c` for
  the hack, `glshim/glx_<name>.c` for each helper copied to
  `xs_support/glx/`. Exclude the copies in all three envs' `build_src_filter`
  and keep `-Isrc/xs_support/glx` in `build_flags`. Never define `HAVE_GL`:
  it adds `glx_context` to `ModeInfo`, which `xlockmore.c` (built without
  it) allocates smaller. Build each helper as its own unit: `tube.h` and
  `normals.h` define clashing types.
- TinyGL draws straight into `canvas->px` at the canvas size, with its
  pixel packer patched to the canvas's byte-swapped RGB565. Test colours
  with exact `rgb565()` values: white looks the same either way round.
- Display list name 0 means "invalid" to hacks (`if (!glGenLists(1)) abort()`)
  and TinyGL handed it out first; the patch starts at 1. Its list buffers
  are 64 slots, not 4,096: each list took 16 KB and 500 lists overflowed
  PSRAM (boot loop, `StoreProhibited` at `0x4000` in `alloc_list`).
- TinyGL counts vertex-array stride in floats and reads the array when a
  display list is replayed; GL counts bytes and reads at the draw call, and
  hacks free the array straight after (`tube.c`, `sphere.c`). Hacks'
  `glVertexPointer` and friends are renamed to `glshim_*` by macros in
  `glshim.h`, and `glDrawArrays` expands at once. The symptom of the old
  behaviour was needles through the tubes.
- The context is freed by the shim: `glshim_open` registers
  `xshim_set_release_hook`, which `xshim_release_pixmaps` (the runner's
  `stop()`) runs. A second `init_GL` replaces the first, which hides a
  missing hook, so test `glshim_is_open()` right after the hack stops.
- `glshim_open` returns NULL for an empty canvas or a failed z-buffer
  allocation only. `glInit`'s own allocations (lists, matrix stacks) are
  unchecked upstream, so running out of PSRAM after the z-buffer crashes there.
- `glDrawArrays` reads every client array as `GL_FLOAT` and ignores the type
  argument: check a new hack's `glVertexPointer` calls before trusting it.
- TinyGL leaves specular lighting off (`zEnableSpecular = 0`) unless the
  application calls `glSetEnableSpecular(1)`, so Gears has no highlights
  and `glMateriali` is invisible without it. Enabling it costs speed (#43).
- TinyGL lacks `glTexGeni`, `glFog*` and `glInterleavedArrays` (#46). The
  header declares `glFog*` and the `GL_SPHERE_MAP` enum; the library defines
  neither.
- TinyGL snaps every vertex to a whole pixel (`zp.x`, `zp.y`) before it draws,
  so a line that moves a little jumps a whole pixel somewhere along its length:
  Unknown Pleasures' flat stretches hopped, which read as flicker. The patch
  keeps the fractional position (`zp.fx`, `zp.fy`) and draws a line with Wu's
  algorithm when a hack enables `GL_LINE_SMOOTH`. Only lines get it; filled
  triangles are still snapped. A line whose two colours differ is drawn plain.
- Smooth lines ignore vertex alpha (`ZB_line_aa` reads only r, g, b), so
  Unknown Pleasures' per-row fade (`glColor4f` with an eased alpha) does not
  happen and every ridge draws at full intensity. Rod approved that look on the
  device and closed the review finding as wontfix.
- TinyGL has no alpha: the blend macro adds colours, ignores the blend
  function's alpha, and decodes pixels as if they were not byte-swapped, so
  it is only right for black and white. A white-on-black frame hides this, and
  smooth (grey) lines did not. The fill wrapper (`gl_draw_triangle_fill` in
  `tinygl_patch.py`) treats `SRC_ALPHA, ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA`, which is alpha 1
  in real GL, as an opaque fill. Other blend functions still use the macro and
  are wrong for any colour but black and white.
- Polygon offset was stored and never read. The fill wrapper applies it:
  `factor` times the polygon's steepest depth slope plus `units` times one
  depth step, pushed away from the viewer. Without it a line drawn on the edge
  of its own filled polygon is erased in dashes. Unknown Pleasures' own
  `glPolygonOffset (0.5, 0.5)` is not enough here: vertices are snapped to
  whole pixels, so a polygon's depth is wrong by up to a pixel's slope in each
  direction, and with only the hack's offset each quad still ate a few percent
  of its own line, a different few each frame. The wrapper adds
  `|dz/dx| + |dz/dy|` whenever an offset is asked for (not for an offset of 0, 0).
  Measured on the host by the second difference of a frame's total brightness
  while the picture drifts a fifth of a pixel a frame: 3,201 at the hack's own
  offset, about 500 (the floor) with the margin. An earlier depth-fighting
  experiment found no effect only because blending made every quad invisible:
  change one thing at a time, and check that the thing under test can act.
- The offset's snapping margin takes the sign of the offset (a negative offset
  pulls toward the viewer, so a positive margin would weaken it), the bias is
  clamped to about +/-2^29, and each shifted vertex depth is clamped to the
  16-bit range with the originals restored exactly: an offset that carried a
  fill past the far plane used to wrap round and beat a nearer fill. Tests use
  a second fill slightly behind the first, because a twin at equal depth wins
  a tie either way and cannot tell the signs apart.
- The clipper keeps lines inside the view volume, and the viewport maps NDC 1 to
  pixel `xsize - 0.5`, so only a viewport larger than the canvas can carry a
  line past its right or bottom edge. The smooth-line plot's guards are
  defensive otherwise; `test_glshim` uses `glViewport(0, 0, 2 * SIZE, 2 * SIZE)`
  to reach them.
- Speed is about 6 us per lit vertex plus about 80 ms a frame (clear 25 ms,
  push 32 ms): Gears runs at 4 to 5 fps for its heaviest layout and about 9
  for light ones. `-O2` for TinyGL and specular lookup tables changed
  nothing; whole-firmware `-O2` crashes the compiler in `braid_single.c`.
  `CLIP_EPSILON` was an exponent literal (`1E-5`), which `float_literals.py`
  leaves alone, so `gl_clipcode` ran a software `double` multiply on every
  vertex; `tinygl_patch.py` now makes it `1E-5f`, which took 5.6 ms off
  CubicGrid's 52 ms step (0.7 us a vertex) and about 3 ms off Morph3D's.
  `gl_shade_vertex` has not been checked for `double` the same way.
- Gears picks a random layout on each start, so a running Gears holds 0.9 to
  2.5 MB. Measure leaks while stopped, not by comparing two running moments.
  `free_gears` never frees `bp->gears`: 40 to 1,500 bytes a start, upstream.
- The host stack figure for Gears (21 KB, unoptimised and under
  AddressSanitizer) is not the board's (2.4 KB used in the spike); the host
  test is a tripwire and the board is the proof.
- `dump_main.c` raw frames are already un-swapped; `rgb565_to_png.py` reads
  them as plain RGB565. Swapping them again gives psychedelic stripes.
- `tools/gl_budget.py` counts vertices, triangles and fill in a private,
  instrumented copy of TinyGL (`instrument()` adds the counters after
  `tinygl_patch.patch_tree`, with the same checked anchors). The firmware's
  TinyGL never has them. Its fill cost is fitted to one Gears scene, so it
  over-predicts few-large-triangle scenes, and lines and points cost nothing
  beyond vertex setup. Add a second calibration point after each GL port.
- TinyGL's `glLightModelfv` copied four floats whatever the parameter, so
  `glLightModelfv(GL_LIGHT_MODEL_TWO_SIDE, one_float)` (Morph3D) read past the
  array: AddressSanitizer's global-buffer-overflow. `tinygl_patch.py` now copies
  four only for `GL_LIGHT_MODEL_AMBIENT`. `glopLightModel` still reads the
  value back as an int from a float slot, which only works because any
  non-zero float has non-zero bits; leave it unless a hack passes 0.
- Morph3D is small and wanders by design: a window (not iconic) build scales
  the object to 0.3 and moves it on a Lissajous path, so it is about 70 px
  across on the 466 px canvas and its position differs frame to frame. It
  cannot be enlarged without patching the hack. It enables two lights and
  two-sided lighting; `docs/gl-budget.md` predicts 6 to 11 fps.
- Dirty rectangle: TinyGL reports the box around everything it draws to
  `glshim_note_box` (hooks in `tinygl_patch.py`: triangles, points, lines,
  text pixels, and `glDrawPixels` as the whole canvas). `glClear` clears only the
  box drawn since the last clear and a swap marks only what was drawn and what
  the clear erased. A new context, and a new clear colour, are full clears. The
  contract: nothing else may draw on the canvas while a GL hack runs (the overlay
  restores what it stamps). A line's hook must order its endpoints before adding
  the margin: `p1.x - 1` to `p2.x + 1` shrinks a right-to-left line's box.
  `tools/gl_budget.py` gets its boxes from `glshim_box_observer` so it cannot
  drift from the firmware's rule.
- `glDrawPixels` keeps its data pointer in a 4-byte `GLParam`, so it cannot draw
  on a 64-bit host (fine on the 32-bit board); it has a patch-level test only.
- A hack's own `*delay` is a pause after each frame and the loop credits only the
  push against it, so it hides speed-ups: Morph3D (40 ms) and Gears (30 ms) were
  held to 10 and 11 to 13 fps until their registered override cut it to 10 ms.
  Check `wait=` in the log before judging a speed-up.
- Measuring on the board: a boot is deterministic (same hack, same layout, same
  windows), so alternate builds and compare window by window; one earlier
  outlier read 54.9 ms against 52.3 and was never explained. CubicGrid (fixed
  8,000 unlit points) and Gears' first layout after boot are the repeatable
  benchmarks; Morph3D's shape is random per boot. To split a frame, add a
  temporary `#if GL_PROFILE == n` early return to a TinyGL function through
  `tinygl_patch.py` and flash with `-DGL_PROFILE=n`; never commit it.
- Overlapping the push with the next frame (core 0 pushing while core 1
  renders) is untried; it needs a second 434 KB buffer, a lock around M5GFX, and
  the PSRAM bandwidth may limit the gain.
## Thin lines in a GL hack

When: a GL hack draws hairlines or fades (Unknown Pleasures) and looks right
in a host frame but flickers on the board. Work down this list, one layer at a
time, and look at the screen (or film) after each; each layer hid the next.

- Lines hop. TinyGL snaps every vertex to a whole pixel, so a drifting line
  jumps. `tinygl_patch.py` keeps the fractional position and draws a Wu line
  when the hack enables `GL_LINE_SMOOTH`. Triangles are still snapped.
- Quads that hide the lines behind them hide nothing, or the picture is
  speckled grey. TinyGL's blend adds colours, ignores alpha and misreads our
  byte-swapped pixels, so `SRC_ALPHA, ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA` is drawn as an
  opaque fill. Smooth lines carry no alpha, so a hack's per-line fade is lost.
- A line drawn on its own polygon's edge is erased in dashes: `glPolygonOffset`
  was stored and never read. The patch applies it, plus a margin for the
  vertex snapping. Check the effect on the host by the second difference of a
  frame's total brightness while the picture drifts a fraction of a pixel; change
  one thing at a time, because blending once made the experiment unable to
  show any effect.
- Pieces of a line vanish for one refresh. The panel scans while the push
  writes, so a seam crosses the picture. Set `sync_to_refresh` on the hack
  (`XLOCKMORE_HACK_SYNCED`); see `.claude/rules/device-display.md` for the
  offset, why it is only valid for a full-frame push, and how to film the
  result. Cost: up to a refresh of latency a frame, so only a hack that needs
  it should ask.
- Budget with `gl_budget.py` but expect it to be off: it has no blend term
  (Unknown Pleasures was predicted at 251 ms and ran at 267, then 197 once the
  fills were opaque). Add the measured row as a calibration point.
- After all that a dimming of about 14% for 25 ms at each push remained (issue
  #68). Do not promise a hack is flicker-free from a host frame or from the
  absence of vanishing lines alone.

The seven rows from CWaves to HexTrail are the CWaves, Vermiculate, Cynosure,
Moire, Moire2, Boing and HexTrail batch (2026-10-11), each from a pinned build
read for 30 to 150 s with Rod's go-ahead to flash while he was away. There is
no idle PSRAM reading for this build (the 7,327,227 above predates the QR
overlay), so "Extra PSRAM" is the drop from 6,989,667 bytes, which Cynosure
and Moire read and which allocate almost nothing; treat it as good to about
10 KB. Free heap was flat in every capture and no stack canary, panic or
reboot appeared.

CWaves' cosines were 4 ms of a 61 ms step in single precision; the rest was
233 two-pixel-wide column fills, each store on a different cache line of the
PSRAM canvas. The picture depends on x only, so the wrapper writes the columns
into row 0 and copies that row down (frames identical to the unmodified hack).
Moire is paced by its own delays, 50 ms between 20-row chunks and 5 s between
pictures, so its fps says nothing about speed: the step fell from 44 to 9.5 ms
a chunk. Cynosure waits 500 ms between frames by design (upstream's
default), as Forest does.

Moire2's first plane code took 54 ms. Skipping one call at a time showed the
plane copies at 26 ms and the expansion at 27 ms, both slowed by 64-bit index
maths on a 32-bit core and, for the expansion, a branch a pixel. Working in
32 bits and a byte at a time took the step to 28 ms, and overriding the hack's
50 ms delay (which waited out all but the 28 ms) took it to 16.2 fps. The
occasional frame that builds new planes takes 96-141 ms.

Boing's scanlines, 208 blended full-width lines, cost about 83 ms of the 171 ms
step; a smaller ball (0.3 for 0.5) saves 13 ms more, so the rest is fixed
(the clear, the wall and the shadow). HexTrail draws every hexagon built so
far, so its step climbs to a ceiling and it restarts; the means above are over
150 s, which covers several cycles. The two GL hacks are below the 15 fps bar
in their registered form (8.3 and 12.7), and Boing is below it by a lot.

Unknown Pleasures' rows are from pinned builds (2026-10-10).

input.new_string:
setup (about 35 us), so `*layers` and `*count` cannot reach 15 fps.
- CWaves (`cwaves_single.c`) fills 233 columns, each a 2 by 466 rectangle, so
  every store lands on a different cache line of the PSRAM canvas: after single
  precision took the step from 95 to 61 ms, 57 of those were the fills and 4
  the cosines. The picture depends on x alone, so the wrapper writes each
  full-height column into canvas row 0 and the draw wrapper copies that row
  down (frames identical to the unmodified hack): 16 ms, 20 fps. Any hack that
  paints thin full-height strips can do the same.
- A single-precision wrapper must watch for a hack that passes the address of
  one of its own `double` locals to a shim function (`rgb_to_hsv (..., &fgs,
  &fgv)` in Moire): the prototype still says `double *`, so the float local is
  written eight bytes and the frames come out as colour noise, with no
  compiler warning. `moire_single.c` defines an adapter before
  `single_precision.h` and maps the name to it. Compare the wrapper's frames
  with the unmodified hack's: they were all different here, and identical once
  the adapter was in. A hack with no decimal literals (Moire) must not be in
  `patch_float_literals.py`, which refuses a file without any.
- Moire and Cynosure are paced by their own delays (Moire draws a 20-row chunk
  every 50 ms and holds each picture 5 s; Cynosure waits 500 ms a frame, which
  is upstream's default), so their fps is low whatever the step is. Cynosure's
  `XCreateBitmapFromData`, which the scorer lists as a gap, is inside a
  `DO_STIPPLE` block that is never defined.
- Moire2 (`moire2_direct.c`, `moire2_planes.h`, built on Halo's planes) keeps
  its four depth-1 pixmaps as bit planes and adds an outline circle, an XOR
  rectangle, an OR/XOR/copy between planes (the GC's `function`, which the shim
  now remembers) and a faster expansion to the window. Upstream's free leaves
  its pixmaps to the X server, and the runner frees only the shim's own, so the
  wrapper frees the planes. The first version ran at 9.6 fps: the plane copy
  and the expansion were 26 and 27 ms, because 64-bit index maths is several
  instructions an operation on a 32-bit core and the expansion branched on
  every pixel. After clipping everything fits an int; a byte table of eight
  pixels written four bytes at a time did the rest (28 ms). The 50 ms delay is
  overridden to 10 ms: 12.6 fps became 16.2.
- Boing and HexTrail are GL (`boing_gl.c`, `hextrail_gl.c`). Boing's 208
  scanlines are blended full-width lines and cost half its step: 5.0 fps with
  them, 8.3 without, so the registry turns them off (`-DBOING_SCANLINES` puts
  them back); the ball size barely matters (0.3 saves 13 ms). HexTrail draws
  every hexagon it has built, so its step climbs from about 19 ms to a ceiling
  and it restarts: use a mean over a cycle (150 s). The grid is `count * 2`
  squared, and a smaller count makes fewer, larger hexagons over the same area:
  mean 5.7 fps at upstream's 20, 9.1 at 10, 12.7 at 6 (registered,
  `-DHEXTRAIL_COUNT=<n>`). Neither reaches 15 fps in a form Rod has not yet
  seen, so both are open for him to keep or drop.

new = {"CWaves", "Vermiculate", "Cynosure", "Moire", "Moire2", "Boing", "HexTrail"}
bad = []
for name, v in sorted(visits.items(), key=lambda kv: (kv[0] not in new, kv[0])):
    psr = [p for _, p in v]
    heap = [h for h, _ in v]
    spread = max(psr) - min(psr)
    drift = heap[-1] - heap[1] if len(heap) > 2 else 0
    flag = ""

    if flag:

    mark = "*" if name in new else " "

print()
print("flagged:", bad)

- CWaves: smooth colour bands sliding sideways. Check the colours are not
  swapped (R and B) against what you expect.
- Moire2: two colours, blue/white or purple/black style interference rings.
  Its expansion to the window is new code: check no stripes, tearing or

- Boing: the Amiga ball and shadow. Colours (red and white ball, magenta

| Hack | Registered | Alternative | Trade |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Boing | scanlines off, 8.3 fps | `-DBOING_SCANLINES`, 5.0 fps | CRT look vs speed |
| HexTrail | count 6, mean 12.7 fps | `-DHEXTRAIL_COUNT=10` (9.1) or 20 (5.7) | finer hexagons vs speed |

The board is on a 25 s rotation build starting at CWaves, so the new hacks come up in order: CWaves, Vermiculate, Cynosure, Moire, Moire2, Boing, HexTrail.

| Hack | fps on the board | What it took |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CWaves | 20 | Single precision, plus one row copied down instead of 233 column fills (the fills were 57 of the 61 ms step). Frames identical to upstream. |
| Vermiculate | about 75 | Only needed `ya_random`. |
| Cynosure | 1.8 | Its 500 ms delay is upstream's own, so the pace is by design. |
| Moire | 4.8 | Also paced by its own delays. Needed the shared-memory image calls, `make_color_ramp` and single precision (step 44 → 9.5 ms). |
| Moire2 | 16.2 | Bit planes with OR/XOR copies built on Halo's. The first version ran at 9.6 fps; fixing 64-bit index maths and a per-pixel expansion, then overriding the 50 ms delay, got it to 16.2. |
| Boing | 8.3 (5.0 with scanlines) | Needed `glOrtho`, which TinyGL has commented out. |
| HexTrail | mean 12.7 (min 9.2) | Needed the arrow-key constants. |

One trap worth knowing: in a single-precision wrapper, Moire passes the address of its own `double` locals to a shim function taking `double *`. That wrote 8 bytes into a 4-byte float with no compiler warning, and every frame came out different until I added an adapter.

**Your choices:**
- **Boing:** scanlines off (8.3 fps) or on (5.0). `-DBOING_SCANLINES` turns them back on.
- **HexTrail:** I registered `count` 6, which gives chunkier hexagons. Upstream's 20 averages 5.7 fps and 10 averages 9.1. `-DHEXTRAIL_COUNT=<n>` changes it.
- **Moire2:** I overrode its delay to 10 ms to get from 12.6 to 16.2 fps.
- **Cynosure:** its licence is the original author's, not jwz's. `check_notices.py` now accepts that wording and `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md` reproduces it.

**Checked:**
- **Host:** 555 native tests and 340 pytest pass, `check_notices.py` passes, and all seven copied hacks are byte-identical to upstream. Frame hashes were pinned after I looked at the frames, and every new shim function was mutation-checked.
- **Device:** a 30-minute soak (five full laps of all 69 hacks) showed no reboot, panic or stack canary. PSRAM was exactly flat on every visit for the seven new hacks. Heap fell about 650 bytes for every hack alike, so that's background drift rather than a leak. Hexadrop's PSRAM varied by 2,520 bytes across laps, which isn't from this batch.

**Not done or not verified:**
- **Colours on screen:** only you can judge them, especially Moire2's new two-colour expansion and Boing's GL colours.
- **Speed backtest:** `docs/speed-backtest.md` is not regenerated. `speed_backtest.py` stops on Hypnowheel because it probes that dropped GL port standalone without `rotator.h`. I haven't checked whether `main` fails the same way.

The seven rows from CWaves to HexTrail are the CWaves, Vermiculate, Cynosure,
Moire, Moire2, Boing and HexTrail batch (2026-10-11), each from a pinned build
read for 30 to 150 s with Rod's go-ahead to flash while he was away. There is
no idle PSRAM reading for this build (the 7,327,227 above predates the QR
overlay), so "Extra PSRAM" is the drop from 6,989,667 bytes, which Cynosure
and Moire read and which allocate almost nothing; treat it as good to about
10 KB. Free heap was flat in every capture and no stack canary, panic or
reboot appeared.

CWaves' cosines were 4 ms of a 61 ms step in single precision; the rest was
233 two-pixel-wide column fills, each store on a different cache line of the
PSRAM canvas. The picture depends on x only, so the wrapper writes the columns
into row 0 and copies that row down (frames identical to the unmodified hack).
Moire is paced by its own delays, 50 ms between 20-row chunks and 5 s between
pictures, so its fps says nothing about speed: the step fell from 44 to 9.5 ms
a chunk. Cynosure waits 500 ms between frames by design (upstream's
default), as Forest does.

Moire2's first plane code took 54 ms. Skipping one call at a time showed the
plane copies at 26 ms and the expansion at 27 ms, both slowed by 64-bit index
maths on a 32-bit core and, for the expansion, a branch a pixel. Working in
32 bits and a byte at a time took the step to 28 ms, and overriding the hack's
50 ms delay (which waited out all but the 28 ms) took it to 16.2 fps. The
occasional frame that builds new planes takes 96-141 ms.

Boing's scanlines, 208 blended full-width lines, cost about 83 ms of the 171 ms
step; a smaller ball (0.3 for 0.5) saves 13 ms more, so the rest is fixed
(the clear, the wall and the shadow). HexTrail draws every hexagon built so
far, so its step climbs to a ceiling and it restarts; the means above are over
150 s, which covers several cycles. The two GL hacks are below the 15 fps bar
in their registered form (8.3 and 12.7), and Boing is below it by a lot.

- `feature/43-gl-speed-experiments`: compile-time flags, all off by default (frame hashes match main; default build differs only by a 4-byte `shade_pending` field in GLVertex and `gl_zalloc_hot`). `GL_PROFILE` (stage cycle counts, `glprof` line after `run`), `GL_LAZY_SHADE` (light and transform normals only for drawn vertices; exact on host; Gears heavy 17,700 to 8,645 lighting calls), `GL_IRAM` (+16 KB IRAM), `GL_INTERNAL_MATRICES`, `PSRAM_AUTOLOAD=1/2/3` (dcache next-line prefetch), and `tools/ab_flash.py` (builds variants once, flashes in turn, tabulates). Late patch anchors live in `LATE_REPLACEMENTS`, hot functions in `HOT_FUNCTIONS` in `tools/tinygl_patch.py`.
- `feature/44-pipes` (worktree `.claude/worktrees/pipes`): `docs/pipes-lab/`, host-only lab built from vendor/. content.text:
Boing is out of the rotation, and the first HexTrail speed-up is built and committed. I haven't run it on the board yet, because I need your go-ahead to flash.

**Boing** is gone from the rotation. I removed it from the registry, the expected list, its frame hash and its leak test, and its wrapper is no longer compiled. The source and notices row stay, and `tools/failed_ports.txt` lists it. The `test_hacks` suite passes with 72 cases, and the stopwatch build compiles. This is commit `806a702`.

**HexTrail** (commit `21f766f`):
- **Why it slows down:**
  - Its draw and tick loops did their colour, size and corner maths in `double`, which the S3 runs in software.
  - Its step time grows because the clear and the push scale with how much of the screen the trails cover.
  - Most of the vertices it submits are transformed and then clipped: about 2,900 per frame at count 6, with about 200 triangles actually drawn.
- **What I changed:** I rebuilt it in single precision with float literals, as I did for CWaves.
  - It passes the addresses of `double` locals to `get_position` and `get_rotation`. In a float build that would write 8 bytes into 4-byte floats, as Moire did, so I added adapters.
  - Frame 100 matches the old build; after that the random walk diverges, so I re-pinned the hash after looking at the frames.
  - Zeroing the rotation `z` in the adapter fails the pinned hash, so the test does catch that bug.
- **What I haven't measured:** the speed-up. `nm` shows the per-hexagon loops no longer call software double, but a few once-per-frame double operations remain. The first step is to see what float alone buys.

**Can I flash a pinned HexTrail build for a 150 s capture?** It would be rotation off, count 6, and I'd compare it with the old mean of 12.7 fps and minimum of 9.2. After that I'd put the board back on the 25 s rotation build. If float alone isn't enough, two ideas remain:
- Skipping the clear and push for the four corners of the round screen, which would cut about a fifth of the fixed cost. That is a runner change every hack would see, so it's yours to decide.
- A cheaper clip test before vertices are transformed.
Yes, flash it and measure HexTrail

content.text:
HexTrail's mean is now 15.3 fps, up from 12.7, and its slowest 5-second window is 10.8 fps instead of 9.2. Boing is out of the rotation. Nothing is pushed, there's no PR, and the board is back on the 25 s rotation build starting at CWaves, without Boing.

**HexTrail on the board** (150 s capture, count 6):

| Build | Mean fps | Worst window | Worst step |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| As ported (`double`) | 12.7 | 9.2 | 76 ms |
| Single precision | 13.0 | 9.6 | 71 ms |
| Single precision, plus depth-clear skip | 15.3 | 10.8 | 59 ms |

- **Single precision:** it barely helped, so the hack's own maths wasn't the bottleneck.
- **The depth clear:**
  - HexTrail clears the depth buffer every frame but never turns depth testing on.
  - Nothing ever reads that buffer, so the clear was a second full-screen fill of PSRAM per frame.
  - The clear now waits until a hack enables depth testing, so anything that does enable it still gets a cleared buffer.
- **Other GL hacks:** this is a change to the shared GL layer. It can only matter to a hack that clears depth with testing off, and every pinned GL frame hash still matches.
- **Tests:**
  - The two new tests (clear skipped while off, clear applied once on) failed before the change.
  - They passed after it, and breaking the deferred clear fails both.
  - 556 native tests and 342 pytest pass.

If you'd like HexTrail's hexagons finer, count 10 should now be closer to the old count-6 speed. I haven't measured it with these two changes, and the build flag is `-DHEXTRAIL_COUNT=10`. Two further ideas remain, but neither is done. One is skipping the clear and push for the corners of the round screen, which every hack would see, so it's your call. The other is a cheaper clip test before vertices are transformed.

**Boing:** it's in `tools/failed_ports.txt` as dropped. The source, notices row and measured rows stay, and the wrapper is no longer built.

The branch now has three new commits on top of the batch: Boing dropped (`806a702`), HexTrail in single precision (`21f766f`) and the depth-clear skip (`bf3937f`).
